roles.label: First commercial role (clinician or graduate moving across)
roles.what: You are being bought on trajectory, not track record. The hiring manager is asking one question all the way through: will this person still be here, and productive, in eighteen months. Clinical credibility is your opening advantage and it expires fast; the moment the conversation turns to numbers, forecasts and losing a tender, you are on the same footing as everyone else.
shape: Recruiter screen, often a recorded one-way video answer set before a human sees you.
Hiring manager interview: motivation, resilience, commercial aptitude.
Final stage: a territory or account presentation, sometimes a role-play call.
themes: Why leave clinical practice
Answer it once, cleanly, in the positive. Any version that centres on what you are escaping reads as a flight risk. Name the thing commercial work gives you that the ward could not.
Evidence of selling aptitude
You have almost certainly sold: a change of practice, a new dressing formulary, a business case for kit. Tell it as a sale, with the resistance named and the decision won.
Resilience and self-direction
No one checks your diary. Show a period where you set your own goals and kept going without supervision.
Commercial literacy
Margin, list price versus contract price, cost per patient, why a trust can want your product and still not buy it.
roles.task: Most often a 90 day plan or a short presentation on how you would approach a named territory. Structure it learn, plan, execute. Put named accounts in it, not adjectives.
plan: Days 1 to 30: product and compliance to competent, systems set up, shadow, meet every account once.
Days 31 to 60: territory analysis, account plans, map decision makers and buying routes.
Days 61 to 90: solo calls, qualified pipeline, first committee submission in flight.
ask: What does good look like at six months for this territory, in numbers.
Who held this territory before me and why is it open.
Which accounts are on framework and which are direct.
sink: Talking about patients and never about revenue.
Describing the product instead of the buying route.
No 90 day plan, or a 90 day plan with no account names in it.

roles.label: Territory sales representative (devices and consumables)
roles.what: A quota, a geography and a list of accounts. The interview tests whether you can hold a number under pressure and whether you understand that in the NHS the person who wants your product is rarely the person who can buy it.
shape: Recruiter screen against the number: last three years, target, attainment, territory size.
Hiring manager: pipeline mechanics, account strategy, loss post mortems.
Final: territory business plan presentation, often plus a role-play call with a clinician or a procurement lead.
themes: Attainment, verifiable
Have the numbers exactly: target, achieved, percentage, rank, and what changed year on year. Vague numbers are read as bad numbers.
A loss you own
Pick a real one, name the decision you got wrong, and say what you changed afterwards. A candidate with no losses has no learning.
Working a committee
Value analysis, drugs and therapeutics, capital group. Show you know a clinical yes is the start of the process, not the end.
Territory discipline
Call planning, segmentation, why you spend Tuesday where you spend it.
roles.task: Territory business plan. Segment the accounts, show where the growth is, show what you will stop doing. A plan that grows everything equally is not a plan.
plan: Days 1 to 30: every A account visited, incumbent position understood, framework position confirmed.
Days 31 to 60: segmented plan agreed with the manager, evaluations opened in two accounts.
Days 61 to 90: first conversions, pipeline built to a multiple of quota, committee submissions dated.
ask: What is the split between framework and off contract business here.
What is the average sales cycle from first evaluation to first order.
Which competitor is strongest in this patch and why.
sink: Numbers that move when you are asked twice.
No view on how the product is actually bought.
Blaming the last rep.

roles.label: Clinical specialist / clinical application specialist
roles.what: You are the reason the product works in their hands. Part trainer, part troubleshooter, part in-theatre support, and increasingly part of the sales team's number even where the job description says otherwise. Ask early how you are measured, because the honest answer varies enormously between companies.
shape: Screen on clinical background and product families.
Technical or clinical interview, sometimes with a product specialist rather than a manager.
Practical: a teaching or training demonstration to a lay panel, and questions on adverse events and escalation.
themes: Teaching under pressure
Explain something technical to someone who does not want to be taught, in theatre, mid list. They will test this.
Scope and boundaries
Where your responsibility stops. When you escalate. What you will not do in a clinical area.
Complaints and vigilance
What you do when a device underperforms in front of a customer, and what your reporting duty is.
Commercial awareness
Whether you spot the opportunity while you are supporting, and what you do with it.
roles.task: A live training demonstration, often on a product you have not seen before, with a short prep window. They are watching your structure and your recovery, not your product knowledge.
plan: Days 1 to 30: product certification, observe with experienced colleagues, learn escalation routes.
Days 31 to 60: solo support in the easier accounts, build a training pack.
Days 61 to 90: named accounts owned, competency signed off, feeding qualified leads to the sales team.
ask: Am I carried on the territory number, and if so, how.
What is the on call and out of hours expectation.
How many accounts, and what is the travel and overnight pattern.
sink: Not asking how the role is measured.
Presenting as clinical staff who happen to work for a company, with no commercial edge at all.
No answer on vigilance and complaint handling.

roles.label: Key account manager
roles.what: Fewer accounts, longer cycles, bigger contracts, and a set of relationships you inherit rather than build from nothing. The step up from rep is measured in stakeholder breadth: you are expected to be credible with a finance director as well as a lead nurse.
shape: Screen on account size and contract value.
Hiring manager: account planning method, stakeholder mapping, contract renewals.
Final: present a real or supplied account plan to a panel, defended under challenge.
themes: Account planning as a discipline
Show a method, not an instinct. Who is in the room, what each of them is measured on, where the money sits, what the renewal date is.
Multi level selling
Evidence of taking a conversation above the clinical user. If every relationship you name is a nurse or a surgeon, you are being interviewed for a rep job.
Contract and renewal management
When you started work on the last renewal, and what you did twelve months out.
Cross functional influence
Pulling in marketing, market access, service, clinical education, and getting them to turn up.
roles.task: An account plan, presented and defended. Expect the panel to attack the assumptions. Bring the number, the timeline and the named people.
plan: Days 1 to 30: meet every named stakeholder, read the contract, find the renewal dates.
Days 31 to 60: refreshed account plans with a growth thesis per account, executive relationship started.
Days 61 to 90: at least one new service line or department opened, renewal work under way.
ask: Which contracts renew in the next eighteen months.
Where does this account sit in the wider ICB or system, and who else buys with them.
What has been tried here before and did not work.
sink: An account plan that is really a call plan.
No relationship above head of department level.
Treating a framework place as a guaranteed order.

roles.label: Business development manager / new business
roles.what: You are hired to open what is closed. Expect the process to test hunting behaviour specifically, because most field sales people are farmers and everyone claims to be a hunter.
shape: Screen on new logo count, not revenue.
Hiring manager: prospecting method, sales cycle length, conversion rates by stage.
Final: a live or simulated first call, plus a market entry plan.
themes: Cold pipeline generation
Where the meetings actually come from. Be specific and unglamorous: sources, cadence, hit rate.
Qualification
How you disqualify. A hunter who never walks away is really a busy person.
Route to market for something new
No framework place, no reference site, no budget line. What is your sequence.
Commercial construction
Pilots, evaluation agreements, risk share, managed service. Whether you can build a deal rather than quote a price.
roles.task: A market entry or new business plan for a named segment, with the first ninety days of activity costed and dated.
plan: Days 1 to 30: define the ideal account profile, build the target list, get the first meetings booked.
Days 31 to 60: qualified opportunities in stage, first evaluation agreed.
Days 61 to 90: first order or first signed pilot, repeatable message proven.
ask: Is there a framework route for this product today, and if not what is the plan.
What is the reference site position.
What is the realistic first year new business number and where did it come from.
sink: Pipeline you cannot break down by stage.
No answer for the no budget, no framework, no reference problem.
Confusing activity with qualification.

roles.label: Market access / health economics / NHS-facing
roles.what: You work on the conditions under which the sale becomes possible: evidence, funding route, guidance, procurement and policy. Almost every question is really testing whether you understand who carries the cost and who banks the benefit, and what happens when those are not the same organisation.
shape: Screen on payer and system knowledge.
Technical interview on evidence and economics, often with medical affairs present.
Final: a value proposition or business case presentation to a mixed commercial and clinical panel.
themes: Who pays and who benefits
The classic NHS problem. Name a case where the saving lands in a different budget from the spend, and say what you did about it.
Evidence hierarchy
What a payer will accept, what they will not, and the difference between clinical effectiveness and budget impact.
Guidance and its limits
What guidance obliges an organisation to do, and what it merely encourages. See the sourced facts panel on this page.
System navigation
ICB, provider, place, regional specialised commissioning. Where a decision on your product actually gets made.
roles.task: Build and present a value case or budget impact model for a named product in a named system. They will check whether your assumptions are defensible, not whether the answer is favourable.
plan: Days 1 to 30: map current evidence, funding routes and gaps by product.
Days 31 to 60: priority payer accounts identified, value dossier and budget impact model refreshed.
Days 61 to 90: at least one payer engagement completed and one internal evidence gap formally escalated.
ask: Which products have an evidence gap the field is already hitting.
How does market access sit alongside sales here, advisory or accountable.
What is the position with national guidance for this portfolio.
sink: Talking clinical benefit with no budget impact.
Quoting guidance without knowing what it obliges.
No feel for the difference between a trust decision and a system decision.

roles.label: Regional sales manager / regional business manager
roles.what: You are hired to make other people's numbers. The interview is about your operating rhythm and your appetite for difficult conversations, and it is usually lost on the second of those.
shape: Screen on team size, team attainment, retention.
Hiring manager and HR: performance management, hiring, coaching.
Final: business plan for the region, plus a role-play of a poor performance conversation.
themes: Turning around a poor performer
One real example, with the timeline, the evidence, and the outcome including the ones you exited.
Coaching in the field
What you do on a field day. If the answer is help close the deal, you are selling, not managing.
Forecast integrity
How you know the forecast is real, and what you do when it is not.
Hiring and retention
Your last three hires: where you found them, and how many are still there.
roles.task: A regional business plan, plus a live performance conversation role-play. The role-play is the test. Be direct, be evidenced, and do not rescue the person from the message.
plan: Days 1 to 30: field day with every rep, read the pipeline, verify the forecast.
Days 31 to 60: regional plan agreed, cadence installed, performance issues formally opened.
Days 61 to 90: forecast trusted, coaching plans running, gaps in the team being recruited.
ask: What is the current team attainment and the spread across the region.
What is the attrition rate and what is behind it.
Where is the forecast currently wrong, and does anyone say so.
sink: Never having exited anyone, and no story about trying.
A field day that is a joint sales call.
No cadence: no one on one, no pipeline review, no rhythm.

roles.label: National sales manager / head of sales
roles.what: You own the national number and the people who carry it. The step up from regional is not more of the same: you are hired to decide strategy rather than execute it, to sit on the leadership team, and to be the person who says out loud that the forecast will miss. Expect the process to be longer, to involve the managing director and often finance and HR, and to test commercial judgement over selling ability.
shape: Recruiter or internal talent screen against national number and headcount.
Country manager or managing director: strategy, structure, forecast integrity, market view.
Panel with finance, HR and often marketing: the business plan, and how you would restructure.
Sometimes a final meeting with the regional or European leadership.
themes: Owning a national number
The full picture: national target, achieved, headcount, revenue per head, and what you did in the year it went wrong.
Structure and coverage
Have you designed a territory structure, not just inherited one. Segmenting the country by opportunity rather than by geography is the answer they are listening for.
Building and losing a team
Hiring at scale, developing managers rather than reps, succession, and the exits. At this level you are asked about the exits directly.
Forecast and board credibility
How you build a number you will defend, how early you flag a miss, and what happened the last time you told a board bad news.
Pricing and margin authority
Where you hold the line on price and where you trade it, and how you stop the field discounting the business away.
Working across functions and above your market
Marketing, market access, service, supply. Plus managing a parent company or a regional head who is not in the UK and does not see the NHS the way you do.
roles.task: A national business plan, presented to a panel. Expect to be asked what you would change in the first six months, how you would restructure coverage, and what you would stop doing. A plan that adds activity without removing any is the commonest failure at this level.
plan: Days 1 to 30: read the number properly, field days with every manager, meet the top accounts, verify the forecast independently.
Days 31 to 60: coverage and structure assessment, pricing and discount review, plan agreed with the leadership team, performance and capability gaps opened.
Days 61 to 90: structure changes under way, cadence installed nationally, recruitment started, a defensible forecast presented to the board.
ask: What is the national number, what was delivered last year, and where did the gap sit.
How much authority does this role have over structure, headcount and price.
What does the parent company expect from the UK, and is that realistic.
Which of the current managers would you want me to keep, and why.
sink: Answering as a bigger regional manager: activity and coaching, no strategy.
No view on structure, only on people.
Never having delivered bad news upwards early.
No grip on pricing, margin or revenue per head.

roles.label: Product / marketing manager
roles.what: You own the portfolio's story, its pricing position and its launch. In medtech and pharma the interview leans hard on commercial numbers and on evidence of working through a field force you do not manage.
shape: Screen on portfolio, launch experience and P and L exposure.
Marketing interview: segmentation, positioning, pricing, launch metrics.
Final: a launch or brand plan presentation, defended commercially.
themes: Launch, end to end
One launch you owned. The number, the timeline, what slipped, and what you would do differently.
Pricing and margin
How the price was set, what the discount policy was, and what you did when the field wanted to break it.
Influence without authority
Getting a field force to actually run the campaign.
Evidence and compliance
Working inside the code, and what that means for claims and materials.
roles.task: Build a brand or launch plan for a named product. Panels look for a defensible segmentation and a clear reason to believe, not a long feature list.
plan: Days 1 to 30: portfolio performance, price position and competitor set understood; field ride outs done.
Days 31 to 60: segmentation and positioning refreshed, plan and budget agreed.
Days 61 to 90: campaign live, field adoption measured, first read on impact.
ask: What is the price erosion picture over the last three years.
How much of the plan is national and how much is left to the region.
Who signs off claims and how long does approval take.
sink: Positioning with no evidence behind it.
No number for anything you have run.
Never having been in the field with a rep.

roles.label: Tender, bid and contracts manager
roles.what: You convert an opportunity into a compliant, winning submission inside someone else's rules and someone else's deadline. The interview is about process discipline, writing quality and commercial judgement on what to bid and what to decline.
shape: Screen on bid volume and win rate.
Technical interview on the public procurement process and evaluation criteria.
Final: a written exercise, usually a short question response scored the way a buyer would score it.
themes: Bid or no bid
How you decide, and a time you argued against bidding and were right.
Answering the question asked
Evaluators score against criteria and weightings, not against how good your product is. Show you write to the mark scheme.
Version control under deadline
Unglamorous and load bearing. How you keep a multi author submission clean at 4pm on submission day.
Commercial and legal judgement
Where you push back on terms, and when you take the risk.
roles.task: A timed written response to a real style tender question. Structure, evidence, word count discipline and direct answering beat eloquence every time.
plan: Days 1 to 30: pipeline of live and forthcoming opportunities built, content library audited.
Days 31 to 60: bid or no bid process agreed, first submissions out.
Days 61 to 90: content library rebuilt around scoring criteria, win rate baselined.
ask: What is the current win rate and how is it measured.
Who owns the pricing decision on a bid, and how fast can it move.
How far ahead do you see opportunities, and from what sources.
sink: Talking about the product instead of the criteria.
No view on bid or no bid discipline.
No examples of a submission you got out under real pressure.

roles.label: Medical science liaison / medical affairs
roles.what: Non promotional, scientific, and firmly separated from sales. The interview tests scientific depth first and the boundary second, and the boundary is where candidates from a commercial background usually fall down.
shape: Screen on qualification and therapy area.
Scientific interview, often a paper discussion or a presentation on a clinical topic.
Final: panel with medical, compliance and commercial, testing the non promotional line.
themes: Scientific depth
One therapy area, properly. Expect to be challenged on trial design, endpoints and limitations.
The promotional boundary
What you can and cannot discuss, unsolicited requests, off licence questions. Get this wrong and the interview is over.
Peer credibility
How you build a relationship with a clinician who has no reason to see you.
Insight, not intelligence
What you feed back internally and what you must not.
roles.task: Present and defend a clinical paper or a therapy area update to a scientific panel, including the weaknesses in the evidence.
plan: Days 1 to 30: therapy area and data on board, compliance training done, key opinion leader map built.
Days 31 to 60: engagement plan agreed, first scientific meetings held.
Days 61 to 90: insight reporting running, advisory or educational activity in the diary.
ask: How is medical affairs separated from commercial here, in practice.
What is the current evidence generation plan.
How is this role measured, given it is non promotional.
sink: Selling in a medical interview.
Presenting a paper without naming its limitations.
No clear answer on unsolicited off licence requests.

specs.n: Vascular Surgery / Peripheral Arterial Disease & Aortic
Urology Devices (Stents, Lasers, Scopes & Stone Management)

r: NHS Supply Chain — Blood Collection Devices (1 lot, 19 suppliers, 9 of them new)
bloodcoll.nt: One lot covering the whole category. It replaced and combined the former Blood Collection Systems and Blood Lancets framework and the Blood Culture Collection Systems framework, so a trust's incumbent may sit on it under a different arrangement than the one they remember. Blood collection is nested under Vascular access in the Hub's speciality list because the same accounts touch both — but the buyer is usually pathology or phlebotomy, not the vascular access team.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Electrodes, Ultrasound Gels, Defibrillation and Related Consumables (9 lots, 37 suppliers). Lot 8 is Defibrillation Electrodes and Pads
cardiology.nt: Nine lots: ultrasound gels, adult ECG electrodes, paediatric/neonatal ECG electrodes, neurology electrodes and needles, pre-wired electrodes, foetal scalp electrodes, abdominal CTG belts, defibrillation electrodes and pads, and related consumables. Defibrillation pads are Lot 8. The set below is the defibrillation and ECG electrode players, not all 37 awarded suppliers.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Skin Cleansing, Disinfection and Hygiene (6 lots, 29 suppliers). Lot 5 is Skin Disinfectant (Medicinal Products), Lot 6 is Pre-operative Skin Preparation
skin-prep.nt: Six lots: patient cleansing wipes, waterless bathing, personal care, antimicrobial cleansing, skin disinfectant (medicinal products) and pre-operative skin preparation. The set below is the skin-antisepsis players, not all 29 awarded suppliers. Note that a 2% chlorhexidine / 70% alcohol applicator is a licensed medicinal product, so it sits in Lot 5 rather than with the wipes.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Examination Gloves (4 lots, 19 suppliers). Lot 1 is 6N Nitrile, Lot 2 Specialised, Lot 3 Vinyl, Lot 4 Latex
NHS Supply Chain — Clinical and Sharps Waste Management (7 lots, 14 suppliers)
NHS Supply Chain — Polymer Aprons (8 suppliers), reference 2023/S 000-014652, Medical and Surgical Consumables
NHS Supply Chain — Polymer Products (5 suppliers), reference 2022/S 171-486016, Medical and Surgical Consumables
NHS Supply Chain — Reusable Clinical and Sharps Waste Management Service (3 suppliers), reference 2025/S 000-078535, Medical and Surgical Consumables
infection.nt: Two routes. Examination Gloves is four lots (6N nitrile, specialised, vinyl, latex) — surgical gloves sit on their own framework and hand hygiene on another again, so a glove conversation and a hand-hygiene conversation are different buying routes even with the same infection prevention lead. Clinical and Sharps Waste Management is seven lots covering sharps and clinical waste containers, swab holders, sharps pads, needle counters and needle/blade removers — and it expires 31/10/2026, so it is close to re-tender.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Anaesthesia Machines, Ventilators, Neonatal Equipment and Phototherapy Systems, Related Accessories and Services (4 lots, 25 suppliers, 8 of them new)
anaesthesia.nt: Capital equipment and its accessories and services, in four lots: anaesthesia machines, ventilators, neonatal equipment and phototherapy. Long replacement cycles and a service tail, so the conversation is usually fleet-level and multi-year rather than consumable-by-consumable. Airway management consumables sit on a separate framework.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Respiratory Solutions (6 lots, 37 suppliers). Lot 5 is Diagnostics
respiratory.nt: Six lots: oxygen therapy, aerosol therapy, respiratory therapy, anaesthesia and resuscitation, diagnostics, and sterile water for humidification. Incentive spirometers are ward-level respiratory therapy — the people who feel a shortage are physiotherapy and enhanced recovery, not procurement.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Renal Replacement Therapies Services, Technologies and Consumables (5 lots, 25 suppliers)
renal.nt: Five lots: dialysis consumables and equipment, home dialysis service, home peritoneal dialysis service, continuous renal replacement and plasma therapies, and managed service. Much of this category is bought as a service rather than a product, so the decision sits with the renal unit and the ICB together, and contracts run long.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Infusion Pumps and Administration Sets and Associated Products (4 lots, 27 suppliers). Lot 3 is Gravity Administration Sets, where blood giving sets sit
bloodtx.nt: ⚠ This framework expires 30/09/2026, so any tender conversation now is really a conversation about its successor — check the procurement calendar before quoting it. Derived, and stated so you can judge it: all seven manufacturers named in MHRA alert DSI/2026/003 (B Braun, Baxter, Becton Dickinson, CODAN, Fannin, GBUK and RPG Medical) appear on this framework's own award list, which is why it is filed as the route to market for transfusion giving sets. The brief itself does not name blood transfusion sets in a lot.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Enteral Feeding, Bile Bags and Associated Products (5 lots, 19 suppliers, 3 of them new)
nutrition.nt: Five lots: enteral feeding syringes and accessories, enteral feeding devices, enteral feeds, giving sets and pumps, and bile bags/Ryles and Levin tubes. Bought by nutrition and dietetics, gastrostomy services and community teams — not by the vascular access people, even though the accounts overlap.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Total Orthopaedic Solutions 3 (3 lots, 98 suppliers, 22 of them new). Lot 1 is Implants and Consumables, which includes bone cement
ortho.nt: Three lots: implants and consumables (12 sub-lots covering hip, knee, extremities, spine, fixation, arthroscopy, bone preparation, power tools, regenerative technology and custom implants), equipment (robotics, navigation, imaging), and services. 98 awarded suppliers — the largest framework the Hub tracks. The set below is the bone cement players plus the alternatives NHS Supply Chain itself names against the current shortage, not all 98.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Surgical Gloves (1 lot, 9 suppliers)
NHS Supply Chain — Electrosurgical Consumables and Related Accessories (6 lots, 33 suppliers, 12 of them new)
NHS Supply Chain — Patient Temperature Management (5 lots, 18 suppliers)
theatres.nt: Three routes, because theatres is not one buying line. Surgical gloves is a single lot with nine suppliers. Electrosurgical Consumables (which replaced the old Diathermy Consumables framework) runs six lots: diathermy plates, pencils, smoke evacuation, argon pencils, suction coagulators and forceps. Patient Temperature Management runs five lots covering forced air warming, blood and fluid warming, temperature equipment, passive warming and sensors — and NHS Supply Chain has said it is renewing that one for a mid-2027 launch, so it is the one to watch.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Laboratory Diagnostics, Point of Care Testing and Pathology Managed Services (7 usable lots, 122 suppliers, 19 of them new). Lot 5 is Laboratory Equipment and Consumables
pathology.nt: Seven lots in use: managed services, blood and cellular sciences, genomics, point of care testing, laboratory equipment and consumables, digital pathology and imaging, and one-stop. 122 awarded suppliers, the second largest framework the Hub tracks. Much of pathology is bought as a managed service on long contracts, so a consumable conversation and an analyser conversation are very different sales. The set below is the histology and consumables end, not all 122.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Advanced Wound Care (18 lots, 56 suppliers, 13 of them new)
wound.nt: Eighteen lots covering hydrogels, gelling fibres and alginates, wound contact layers, super absorbents, foams, hydrocolloids, IV and film dressings, burns and scar management, irrigation, debridement, adhesive removers, skin protectants, compression bandages and adhesive tapes. Developed with clinicians and aligned to the National Wound Care Strategy Programme. General wound care, wound closure and negative pressure wound therapy each sit on their own separate frameworks — check which one a product is actually on before quoting a route.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Endoscopy, Endourology and Oncology Ablation Consumables and Associated Products (3 lots, 58 suppliers, 17 of them new)
endoscopy.nt: Three lots: endoscopy, endourology and oncology ablation. Consumables only — the scopes themselves and the washer-disinfectors that reprocess them are bought on separate frameworks, and decontamination capital is under Sterile services here. A trust's endoscopy unit therefore buys from three different routes, which is worth knowing before you promise to 'sort endoscopy' for them.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Decontamination Capital Equipment, Associated Accessories and Services (3 lots, 20 suppliers, 4 of them new)
ssd.nt: Three lots: endoscopy decontamination units, central decontamination units, and reverse osmosis water treatment. This is capital equipment with a long service tail, so the sale is a multi-year estate conversation with SSD and estates, not a consumable one. The chemistry that runs through the machines is bought separately.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Complete Ophthalmology Solutions 3 (12 sublots, 53 suppliers, 21 of them new)
ophthalmology.nt: Twelve sublots covering ophthalmic capital equipment, surgical consumables, intraocular lenses, procedure packs, instruments, solutions, ocular products, glaucoma equipment, graft materials, contact lenses, low vision aids, and services and software. Cataract surgery is the highest-volume elective procedure in the NHS, so the intraocular lens and procedure pack lots are where the volume sits.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Intravenous Cannula and Associated Products
NHS Supply Chain — Central Venous Catheters and Associated Products
vascular.nt: Covers PICCs, CVCs, securement (incl. SecurAcath) and tip confirmation under the CVC framework; peripheral cannulae under the IV Cannula framework.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Urology and Bowel Management (18 lots, 57 suppliers). It absorbed the former Stoma Care and Accessories framework
NHS Supply Chain — Male Intra-Urethral Catheter with Magnet Control (1 supplier), reference 2026/S 000-013783, Medical and Surgical Consumables
continence.nt: Acute route above (Lot 1 internal catheters, Lot 2 sheaths, Lot 3 drainage bags). In the community, most continence products are prescribed via Part IX of the Drug Tariff — a separate route with its own listing process.

r: NHS Supply Chain — CT Scanners and Associated Options and Related Services (6 categories, 8 suppliers)
NHS Supply Chain — Contrast Injectors, Consumables and Associated Options and Related Services (5 suppliers), reference 2021/S 000-007768, Diagnostic Equipment and Services
imaging.nt: CT only, and only eight suppliers — one of the most concentrated fields in this tool. Six categories: general, advanced and premium CT, wide-bore for radiotherapy simulation, and mobile scanners for head-and-neck or whole-body. Every other imaging modality is bought on its own separate framework (MRI, bone densitometers, contrast injectors, angiography and hybrid theatres, digital diagnostics), so check which one a product is actually on before quoting a route. This is capital with a long service tail — the sale is an estate and business-case conversation, not a consumable one.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) Endoscopes and Associated Options and Related Services (4 product categories, 7 suppliers)
ent.nt: Seven suppliers, the smallest field in this tool — organised by product category rather than lots: fibre optic endoscopes, intubating endoscopes, video endoscopes, and video processors and light sources. NHS Supply Chain notes some suppliers may have outstanding conditions of award. ENT scopes are reprocessed like any other flexible endoscope, so the decontamination framework under Sterile services is the other half of this account's spend.

r: NHS Supply Chain — Audiological Diagnostics, Implantable Devices and Services (2 lots, 15 suppliers)
audiology.nt: Two lots: audiological implantable devices (cochlear implants, bone-conduction and middle-ear devices) and audiological diagnostics (the test equipment). They are very different sales — an implant is a surgical, commissioned, per-patient decision made with an ENT surgeon and a specialist centre; diagnostics is departmental equipment. Hearing aids themselves are procured separately by services rather than through this framework.

Rolling programme of framework agreements; individual frameworks are re-tendered on their own cycles

pharma.nt: ⚠ MEDICINES DO NOT GO THROUGH NHS SUPPLY CHAIN. Everything else in this tool is bought on an NHS Supply Chain framework with a public catalogue and a published award list. Medicines are not. They are bought on NHS England MPSC frameworks — the team formerly called the Commercial Medicines Unit — which "establishes the commercial arrangements to enable the purchasing of medicines prescribed in NHS hospitals in England". The named framework categories are: generic medicines used in hospital; generic medicines used in primary care; clozapine; sevoflurane; tranche medicines; national branded category; intravenous fluids; influenza vaccine; aseptically prepared chemotherapy and monoclonal antibodies for cancer; low molecular weight heparins and fondaparinux; hereditary angioedema; blood disorders including haemophilia A and B; and patent-expiring medicines. ·· TWO THINGS THAT CHANGE HOW YOU SELL. First, PRICES ARE CONFIDENTIAL: only "authorised NHS pharmacy staff" can see them, via the MPSC web catalogue. There is no public price list to work from and no published award list, which is why there is no comparison table below. Second, and the one most people get wrong: INDEPENDENT SECTOR PROVIDERS ARE EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE for MPSC framework prices — NHS England's published position lists them as out of scope "irrespective of the volume of NHS patients supported", alongside general primary care providers and community pharmacies. So a private hospital cannot buy at these prices even when treating NHS patients; it buys through wholesalers and its own group arrangements. A small number of private patients treated inside NHS organisations are the narrow exception, and even then the purchasing point "must request approval to purchase at MPSC framework prices from the relevant framework holder in advance". ·· The services AROUND medicines — homecare, pharmaceutical wholesale, aseptic isolators and cleanroom consumables, radiopharmaceuticals, contrast media, pharmacy robots and specialist couriers — are a different route again, run by NHS collaborative procurement organisations. That is often the more accessible way in for a supplier who is not a medicines manufacturer. ·· READING THE RECALL CLASSES, in the MHRA's own words from its Guide to Defective Medicinal Products, because the class tells you how hard to push and most people guess. A National Patient Safety Alert, equivalent to the old Class 1, means "the defect presents a risk of death or disability". Class 2 means "the defect may cause mistreatment or harm to the patient, but it is not life-threatening or serious". Class 3 means "the defect is unlikely to cause harm to the patient, and the recall is carried out for other reasons, such as non-compliance with the marketing authorisation or specification". Class 4 is a Notification, not a recall — a "Caution in Use" notice "where there is no threat to patients or no serious defect likely to impair product use or efficacy", generally minor defects in packaging or printed materials. ·· THE NON-OBVIOUS ONE, and the reason to read Class 4s rather than skip them: the MHRA also issues them "where a defect has been identified but due to supply concerns product cannot be recalled". A Class 4 can therefore be a SUPPLY signal wearing a labelling headline — the product is defective enough to warn about and too scarce to pull. ·· Note too that most recalls are Class 2 or 3 and stop at pharmacy or wholesaler level: the MHRA's own guidance says patient-level recalls are rarely required at that risk level because "recalls may present a greater risk to the patient than continuing treatment". So a Class 2 landing in a hospital pharmacy is a stock and substitution problem, not a ward-level emergency.
